title: Initiative Measure IL26-001: Parental Rights in Public School

context.text: Citizen initiative to the Legislature. The Legislature did not act on it before the 2026 session ended, so under state law it was placed on the November 3, 2026 ballot; the Secretary of State certified it on August 21, 2026. It would re-enact the 2024 parental-rights law that the Legislature had passed as Initiative to the Legislature 2081 and then amended in 2025.

question.text: Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 concerns parental rights relating to their children in public school. This measure would repeal amendments to a statute listing certain rights of parents and guardians of public-school children and re-enact the law as it was originally enacted by Initiative to the Legislature 2081. Should this measure be enacted into law? Yes / No

summary.text: Per the Attorney General's explanatory statement, the measure would undo the 2025 Legislature's changes to RCW 28A.605.005 and restore the list of parent and guardian rights as enacted in 2024. Among the changes: school records would have to be produced within ten business days instead of 45; parents would have a right to prior notification when non-emergency medical services are offered to their child; the right to immediate notice of criminal action and law enforcement involvement would no longer be limited to school property and school hours; schools would have to notify parents if a child is removed from school without parental permission; the opt-out notice list would add topics such as a child's sexual experiences or attractions; and the right to opt out of comprehensive sexual education would be rewritten as a right to written notice and the option to opt out of instruction on topics associated with sexual activity. The statute's non-discrimination language would be replaced with a right to assurance that the school will not discriminate based on the family's sincerely held religious beliefs, and provisions on harassment complaints, enrollment rights, language access, special education and the no-private-right-of-action clause would be removed. The Office of Financial Management says the initiative would have no fiscal impact on the state and that school districts may incur minor, indeterminate costs to update policies.

measure.yesMeans: Repeals the 2025 amendments to the parents' rights statute for public-school children and re-enacts the law as originally enacted in 2024 by Initiative to the Legislature 2081, with the changes described in the Attorney General's explanatory statement.
measure.noMeans: Leaves in place the parents' rights statute as amended by the 2025 Legislature (RCW 28A.605.005).

argumentsFor.text: Argument for (written by teachers, a superintendent and parent advocates): “These rights include access to their child’s instructional materials and student records, notice of medical services, opt-outs from certain activities and instruction, and immediate notification when law enforcement questions their child or their child is removed from campus without parental permission.”

Argument for: “School staff remain mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse or neglect. Privacy for vulnerable children remains paramount. But safeguards designed for children at risk should not become a default policy of withholding information from all parents.”

Rebuttal of the argument against (same authors): IL26-001 “expressly states that schools ‘shall not be required to release’ mental health counseling records when a parent is the target of a child abuse or neglect investigation; requires ‘immediate notification’ if a criminal action is deemed committed against or by their child; and contains zero mandates placing students in danger.”

argumentsAgainst.text: Argument against (written by State Sen. John Lovick, the Washington Coalition Against Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault, the Washington State Nurses Association, the League of Women Voters of Washington and others): “This poorly written measure further endangers vulnerable child abuse victims by requiring schools to hand over sensitive information to parents under criminal investigation for raping, abusing or otherwise harming their own child.”
Argument against: “An unintended consequence of IL26-001 is ending Washington’s legal requirement that schools immediately notify parents when the crime is reported.”
Argument against: the measure “forces schools to knowingly put LGBTQ+ kids in increased danger of violence and homelessness by outing them to potentially abusive families.”

researchNotes: The official voters' pamphlet does not publish a 'a yes vote means / a no vote means' statement for this measure; the yesMeans/noMeans text is derived strictly from the Attorney General's explanatory statement. The pamphlet's for/against statements are written by committees appointed under state law; the Secretary of State states it 'is not responsible for the content of statements or arguments' (WAC 434-381-180). Arguments are quoted from the Whatcom County edition of the voters' pamphlet; the statewide-measure pages (9-22) were compared with the Spokane County edition and are identical, and the Secretary of State publishes no separate English statewide edition. The two sides disagree about the measure's effect on notification of parents when a child is a crime victim; the Attorney General's statement says the measure would remove the right to immediate notice of alleged abuse or assault by a school employee or contractor and would remove the limit of school property/hours on criminal-action notice. The sponsoring organization was not confirmed from a source loaded for this entry.
